utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President. Mr. President, Colonel Beara is scheduled to testify tomorrow at 9.00 and I received an e-mail from his lawyer yesterday asking that his appearance be postponed until the Appeal Chamber determines the issue of whether a person whose case is pending on appeal can be compelled to testify. That's an issue that's now before the Appeals Chamber in the case of General Tolimir. So we don't disagree that it's reasonable for Colonel Beara who is in the same position, to have -- not be required to testify until that issue is resolved. So we join in the request of Mr. Beara's lawyer that his appearance be postponed until that issue is decided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you like to make any observations, Mr. Tieger, about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We think that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the issue but in the meantime we will not hear Mr. Beara's evidence tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Grujic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The same goes for both me and you today as well, we should speak slowly, clearly and pause. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D1417, please? I don't think this is what I asked for. I believe that that's not that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Number again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D1417. Maybe it's 14 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What we saw was 1D1417.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D -- I see. Thank you. That has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this document is, just tell us that, who issued it and what does it pertain to? Please enlarge the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Ministry of the Interior, the service from Valjevo sent this to the district public Prosecutor's office in Sabac. This is a criminal report against Dusan Vuckovic and Vojin Vuckovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go further down to see what this shorter passage says? Do you see the three lines on the bottom?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, at the bottom. Due to reasonable grounds to suspect that as co-perpetrators they committed the crime of war crime against ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Against who?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the next page now, please? The last paragraph, please, where it says the Yellow Wasps, Zute Ose, and Vuckovic, Dusan as a member of that unit, what was it that they organised, torture, killing, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely, that's what I said yesterday, that when I talked to a particular official I actually said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the next page now, please? Do you remember what you said, how many persons had they killed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know exactly how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the last paragraph here, around the middle, it says, 19 persons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was established at the trial in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that they had taken these steps?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out only later, from the newspapers, TV, et cetera, when they were brought in for the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. D2269, could we please take a look at that now? Could you tell us briefly what this is and what it pertains to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an indictment against Dusko Vuckovic and Vojin Vuckovic, two brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now have D482? Can you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a judgement on the basis of which they were convicted for the crimes they committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The supreme court of Serbia actually increased the sentence on appeal because the prosecutor appealed.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from eight to 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Not going into the expeditiousness of the judiciary in the Balkans, are you on the whole satisfied with the solution that was ultimately reached through judiciary channels?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is based on the justice of God, as we say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about volunteers. Can you tell us whether you knew at the time how the law regulated the question of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew a little bit, as much as I could. I think the Supreme Commander, the government, or someone from Yugoslavia or Serbia, I cannot tell you exactly, reached a decision to the effect that volunteers are considered to be the regular army and shall be part of the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 50 it was suggested to you the learned Prosecutor spoke about volunteers, and then in her question she changed that and she said that you had probably welcomed the paramilitaries. Can you tell us whether you did welcome paramilitaries or whether you welcomed volunteers and what did they say when they came? Did they say they were volunteers or paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part they came as volunteers who came to help their people, their people who were imperilled in Bosnia, in Zvornik, at the time. We took them in as our very own and we sent them to the regular command of the TO and then they were deployed in certain units where there was a shortage of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did they become paramilitaries? Did all volunteers become paramilitaries and through which act did that happen?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. God forbid. There were many of them that fought honourably and even laid down their lives in the defence of the Serb people. They became paramilitaries when they got out of the chain of command that existed there under the command of the Territorial Defence, when they no longer obeyed the command of the Territorial Defence, when they would just wander about and do whatever they pleased, then they were not the military any longer, then they were paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 46, you were asked about mobilisation. You explained that this was some kind of a test mobilisation that you had declared on the 5th of April, 1992. Can you remind us when it was that Alija Izetbegovic declared general mobilisation for all municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was on the 4th of April. I'm not quite sure of the date. Alija quite simply declared that as president and Supreme Commander of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He declared this general mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we briefly take a look at 1D43108?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Hasn't been released, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute of patience, please. Thank you. New number, 1D44050. New number. It seems that there is no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read who it was that wrote this and can you read the title?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was written by some Hasan Efendic on the 17th of November, 1999, and it says development and growth of defence liberation forces from 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have page 3 in e-court, maybe it's even page 2, we'll see. Can we have -- first, could we have the second page, or no, the third one. Yes. Now, please take a look at this long paragraph, the third one, but please just tell us this: The Presidency at the 94th session on the 3rd of April --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- considered several requests for mobilisation, units in their area, and then a conclusion was reached at the session held on the 4th of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Last sentence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "To carry out mobilisation ..."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot find it: "To carry out mobilisation of the entire reserve police force of the SRBH in compliance with previous decisions of the Presidency of the government of the SRBH." In my opinion it is one of a very good but belated decisions which means that this should have been done earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When they say all the municipalities, did that include Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can this be admitted for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did the witness read out something at all from this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a few sentences.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I cannot find it, to carry out mobilisation of the entire reserve police for the SRBH in compliance with previous decisions. Is this part of this document or the witness's evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I was reading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was read out. It's part of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just -- of course, it can be marked. I just want to note that we may have objections based on a lack of foundation with this document. We will wait to see the translation first and make our submissions in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3731.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 38 of yesterday's transcript, it was suggested to you with relation to what you had said that you were reporting that Jovo Mijatovic as a deputy was submitting reports to the central office. Can you tell us is there any written report and can you tell us during which period was Mijatovic able to go to Pale?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was under blockade initially. I don't know for how many months, but I don't remember when the road was unblocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any written reports?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very rarely. It was him who mainly communicated with the central office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On pages 35, you were asked about the document called A and B, and you heard quotations from the trial in Belgrade and it was put to you that you believe that the instructions had come directly from Radovan Karadzic. Can you tell us who from Zvornik attended the meeting on the 19th of December, 1992 [as interpreted], of the SDS, who attended the meeting, who brought this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Jovo Mijatovic who went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were not there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't believe. I may have been there but I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mijatovic explain how he received this paper and how it was adopted and how the voting was done?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, could you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovo Mijatovic said that the document had been given to him by the secretariat to take it to Zvornik, and he offered no explanation as to whether there was any voting on it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The accused referred to a meeting on 19 December 1992, or at least that's how it came out in translation. I think it was intended to be 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it's a matter of translation. I did say "1991."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 25, line 18, there is an ambiguity. You said since this unit was lined up, and then you spoke about what the Serbs undertook and what was happening after the unit had been lined up. Which unit did you have in mind, because it's not clear?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the unit of the Patriotic League lined up on this 17th of October, 1991, in the village of Godus under full combat equipment and they were using nationalistic slogans that had a threatening tone aimed at the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 24, there was mention of the way in which the weapons were distributed to the local boards. However, there is no such thing in the Serbian original. Was -- were the weapons distributed to the party boards?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, it was distributed to individuals in each village, so that then they have a couple of weapons in order to defend themselves in the event of an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you speak English?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I speak a little German.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During these interview, did you have your own interpreter who was controlling their interpreter?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 23, you wanted to explain something about the procurement of weapons in the Serbian version but you were interrupted and then I had to do it. Could you kindly tell us what it was that you wanted to say about the weapons obtained by the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that the Serbian side procured weapons individually on the black market. You said that even I bought a rifle for myself on the black market and I said that only one batch of weapons arrived with the aid of Mr. Spasojevic and that it was distributed to the villages a couple of pieces each, and this is as far as the arming go. At the beginning of the war, when Arkan was there already, since the army didn't want to return the weapons to the TO that were kept in their custody --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, the interpreters again are unable to follow you. Could you repeat from "... since the army didn't want to return the weapons to the TO that were kept in their custody." That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm sorry, Mr. President. Since the weapons of the TO staff was in custody of the JNA and the JNA did not want to return the weapons, then Arkan called General Savo Jankovic by phone and he nearly threatened him that if he didn't send the weapons to Zvornik, he would come over himself to take it over. Two or three hours later Savo Jankovic sent the weapons and they arrived at the TO staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us this: It was suggested to you that the Muslims of Kozluk had signed that they were leaving voluntarily but these were false signatures. When they crossed the border, were they able to tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were allowed to tell the truth any place, in Kozluk, in Serbia, in Serbia, to the media, they thanked the authorities of Zvornik for having been treated in a humane way. They were allowed to leave without any problems, that they were provided with the means of transportation, et cetera. However, later on, somebody saw an opportunity of -- to qualify this voluntary departure as a forced expulsion or forced relocation. This is totally untrue. There was no forced relocation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have now Prosecution Exhibit P106? I believe we have an English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this is the Serbian commissioner for refugees and they reviewed written statement of 1.822 persons from Kozluk who stated that they wanted to leave Yugoslavia without any pressure whatsoever and to go to West European countries, and in conclusion it says that the above given statements were given on their own behalf. What could possibly have forced them to lie to the authorities of Serbia since there were now people from Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please start his answer from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is true. This is not a lie at all. These people signed the statement that they were leaving voluntarily and they indeed left voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, did the Yellow Wasps ever return to Zvornik? Were they allowed to return and were they welcomed after the arrest?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, following the arrests, some of them did return, but very soon thereafter they were chased out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at D1418?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a list of persons banned from entering the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether this ban was complied with?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot guarantee this because I was not in a position to control what the police and the army were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last question: You mentioned that people were called to come back. Did this call refer to the Serbs and tell us to whom did it refer?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It referred to all the citizens of Zvornik who had left the territory, both the Muslims and the Serbs, to go back to their homes and to their places of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that a number of people from both communities did return. What was the position of the Muslim leadership of Zvornik municipality to those people?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslim leadership of Zvornik had already fled. They were not there on the spot in order to communicate with them. However, the people returned, nobody bothered them, they were able to exercise all their rights and they were treated fairly by all the organs of the municipality of Zvornik, like the municipality organs and the police.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the number of the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P01622 [as interpreted]. D, Defence; not P.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Take a look at this proclamation adopted on the 8th of May, 1992, by the leadership of the Muslim municipality.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is their leadership in exile and this is a letter addressed to their people, calling upon them as it says in paragraph C, Muslims, rise to the arms, go to the woods or a free territory, place yourselves at the disposal of the Territorial Defence. They even called upon the people who remained in Zvornik to go to the woods to join them and to take arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please read the next sentence where you stopped after "Territorial Defence of the municipality."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Do not go back to the town," or, I think, "villages," but, rather --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, it says "Do not go ..."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot read it. Oh, yes: "Do not go to work or get involved in any other business activities that would give legitimacy to the occupation power." That means that they are addressing all the workers and administrative staff to refrain from going to work in order to deprive the incumbent authorities of their authority and power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Regarding refugees, you were asked a question and you said that there were 20.000 refugee Serbs from the Federation. Where did you accommodate those people?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's a small figure. Somebody wrote the wrong number. We had from 35.000 to 40.000 refugees pass through Zvornik from the beginning until the end of the war. In the beginning, we would put them in schools. Some families also took people in. They would take them and place them in their homes and then when there was no more room, then we formed a commission which used houses abandoned by Muslim citizens. Then all the property was inventoried in the house, and then a family would be allowed to use those housing facilities temporarily so that when the family would leave that accommodation, they would have to hand back everything that was originally listed as being in that flat or house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did it happen, Mr. Grujic, that the local population unlawfully occupied housing units, and in that case what did you do?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such cases and we reacted energetically. We would return them back to their property or home immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in our legal system, what is that procedure called when somebody is denied the right to move in?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not denied in any way. It's not your house so get out. You have your own house. You don't need another one. We did not have any proceedings and drag them through the courts. It was an extraordinary situation, extraordinary times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you see any difference between "iseliti" and "proterati," "move out" and "expel"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Move out and return someone to their own house is one category. Expel is something else. It means to seize somebody's home and their property.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To be clear, tell us how to spell those two words in B/C/S, "move out" and "expel."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking me, right? "Iseliti" is i-s-e-l-i-t-i; and "to expel," "proterati," is p-r-o-t-e-r-a-t-i.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you repeat the number, 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3982.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what this document is that you issued, the document on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is intended as instruction to free up a sports hall or a sports centre, as we called it. We used it as a reception section. This is where we received all the refugees. That was their first point of contact. And then after that the commission would assign them accommodation depending on the number of family members. They would be placed in empty housing and they would get a temporary decision allowing them to use somebody else's property.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did there occur anywhere an unlawful change of ownership in -- of property and was that property later restored to their rightful owners?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Such cases did not take place, but the temporarily used property, all of it, was eventually returned to their rightful owners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we -- I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3732, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I now have P147A -- P1478, Mladic's diary, Serbian version, 252, English version, 254. Can we please look at the typed pages? Well, it's possible that it's already typewritten. Serbian 252, English 254.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, we are talking about the second paragraph from the top, "We he had to evict some of the people also for the sake of our 'heroes' who fled from Kovacevici." Could you please explain what these quotation marks indicate and what does that mean, this "Kovacevici"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please tell me again where? I cannot find the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's the left-hand side, top part of the page.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Believe me, I really don't know what he meant here, what he says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how do you understand this word "heroes" in quotation marks who fled from Kovacevici?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means deserters who fled from the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you evict Muslims or your locals who were not permitted to illegally occupy somebody else's property?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only those who had their own house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, in fact, I think Dr. Karadzic has to move on here. He said -- he asked him what this meant, and the witness said, "... believe me, I really don't know what he meant here," and then he asks a leading question looking for a particular answer. He's asked the question, the witness in a non-leading way, the witness says he doesn't know. I think he should move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could we look at the previous page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how you understood the tone and the sense of this last sentence, at the bottom, "We were the most active in evicting Muslims"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is in quotation marks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you understand it and do you recall him speaking about it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall him talking about it. Perhaps I had gone out for that. I don't think that I can answer this honestly and adequately, this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And they translated it, and I'm going to read it to you now.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is an error, erroneously written down. I wasn't present. I really cannot answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say here, "iseljavanje," "moving out," or "proterivanje," "expel," "expulsion"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It can be moving out at their request. Perhaps assistance was given to those people at their request to go to the territory under Muslim control or to a foreign country. If that is what he meant, then it's all right. If he meant something else, then really I don't know. I couldn't say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Perhaps this is over but Dr. Karadzic is now providing his own interpretations of words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I find that his comments is fair. It's referring to the difference between "iseliti" and "proterati."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Right, except that he translated them himself into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. This passage was shown to the witness in your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My concern is that Dr. Karadzic provided his own translations from B/C/S into English in the question. If he has a concern with the translation as it's written here, he should go through the appropriate channels to seek a revision. That's my concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the witness confirmed or agreed with Mr. Karadzic's observation as to the meaning of "iseliti" and "proterati" earlier on. So on that basis I will allow Mr. Karadzic to continue that question, but let's continue. The Chamber is -- the issue is noted by the Chamber. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. Mr. Grujic, thank you. The Defence rests. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, could you tell us the position you took during the war? I take it you were the president of the SDS party but I just a minute ago I saw the position as the president of the temporary government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to give a broader explanation. I was the president of the municipal board of the SDS, but just before the war broke out, when Arkan arrived, we continued to negotiate with the Muslims about a peaceful resolution in Zvornik. At no cost did we even consider that there would be a conflict. That's why we continued with the negotiations. The negotiations were conducted in the Mali Zvornik hotel. Arkan found out about it, went to the hotel in Mali Zvornik and acted very cunningly. He entered the room where the negotiations were underway and he beat up our Serbian negotiators, the president of the Municipal Assembly, Jovo Mijatovic, and the Executive Board president, Jovo Mijatovic [as interpreted], in front of the Muslims, and he ordered them to place a white flag the following morning at 7.00 a.m. on the municipal building and if this does not happen, the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear everything that he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then when -- I'm just coming to that, I'm just coming to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just tell us your position you took during the war.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely what I wanted to say. Now, since Jovo Ivanovic [as interpreted] was beaten up, he submitted his resignation as president of the Executive Board at that same moment and went to the factory to work. Since then that post was empty, and it was not possible to convene an assembly that would elect the Executive Board president. Then the Crisis Staff chose me to be acting president of the Executive Board, so that is why I was there temporarily until the assembly had the opportunity to convene and elect a new president of the executive -- of the municipal board and that's how I ended up carrying out that duty for a couple of months or so, until the Yellow Wasps attacked. So I was acting president of the Executive Board for that period, and that's how that came about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it that you continued to be the president of the municipal board of the SDS in 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was later replaced as president of the municipality and president of the municipal board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were the president of the municipality of Zvornik in 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No, no, no, no. I was actually replaced already in late 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what were you in 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the president of the municipal board for a couple of months. I continued to be at the post of the party president. I didn't have any other posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Neither the Prosecution nor the Defence asked you a question about 1995. So I'd like to ask you to tell us what you know about the killing of prisoners who were taken to the Zvornik area after the Srebrenica had been fallen.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, I went back to my private business. I was managing my private bakery, bakery, pastry shop so I did not get involved in any kind of government organ. What I heard from citizens, these stories, I think there is no point in me repeating that. There were different stories going around, none of them would really be relevant enough for me to tell you about them here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Then unless my colleagues have a question for you, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Grujic. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you just permit me, please, to greet my president?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He must have accepted your will already so that will not be allowed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While the next witness is being called in, the Chamber is seized of the motion from the Prosecution to redact some paragraphs of the next witness's statement. Considering that some parts of the paragraphs referred to in the Prosecution motion contained detailed evidence about events in Doboj which is not a municipality charged in the indictment, the Chamber grants the Prosecution motion in part in and order to redact the paragraphs 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 31 and 34, and it denies the remainder of the motion; i.e. paragraphs 12, 18 and 19 will remain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ninkovic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Ninkovic, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule of evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal. That is Rule 90(E). Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony, compelled in such circumstances, would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]Good day, Mr. Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like us both to bear in mind that we should speak slowly and pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ninkovic, did you give a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we please have 1D9230 in e-court. You see the statement before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please just pause a bit more before you start answering.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page so that he can identify his signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers basically be the same as those contained in this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: They would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement, Your Excellencies, according to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will deal with the associated exhibits separately. Subject to that redaction on which the Chamber has just ruled, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3733, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have presented 18 associated exhibits, five of which are not on our 65 ter list which we would add -- ask be added since we did not have all those documents at the time we interviewed this witness. Two of those documents have now been ruled out by virtue of the redaction so we are offering 16 associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will tell the numbers of the exhibit the Chamber finds some issues with. 1D9231; 1D26075; 1D26097; 1D26103, referred to in para 38; 65 ter 22049, referred to in para 43; 30012, referred to in paragraph 32. The Chamber finds them either not forming a part -- an indispensable and inseparable part of the statement or not relevant to the case of the accused. So in order for the Defence to tender them, it should lead live as well as showing the relevance of those documents. Otherwise, do you have any objection to the remaining associated exhibit, Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No objections to the remaining associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be admitted and be assigned exhibit number in due course by the Registrar. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out the summary of Mr. Milan Ninkovic's statement in the English language. [In English] Milan Ninkovic is one of the founders of the SDS and was the leader of the Serbs in Doboj. He served as a deputy of the National Assembly president and was -- deputy in the National Assembly and was appointed deputy president of the commission for national defence and control of the work of the State Security Service. At the end of the war, he became minister of defence. At the time of the appearance of the SDA and the HDZ, Serbian people in BH had no intention of becoming politically active or uniting on ethnic principles because it was assumed at the time that the Serbian people could express their cultural and national interests through the Prosvjeta educational and cultural association. Before the founding of the SDS, there was not a single political party or organisation among the Serbian people which could represent its interests. At the first multi-party elections in 1990, the SDS won majority of the municipality -- in the municipality of Doboj, as well as the region around it. As for the national level, the SDS was involved in a special struggle against majority voting or outvoting of the coalition of the two other peoples which was noticed as early as in 1991. The Serbian people were waging a great and difficult fight to remain in Yugoslavia because the secessionist intentions of the Muslims and Croats were obvious. The referendum for the independence of BH was conducted without including the Serbian population and BH was recognised on the same day as the Muslim holiday of Bajram. In late 1991 and early 1992, the Serbian people were fighting to remain a constituent people in BH and within their ethnic entities. This is the reason why the Serbs accepted the Cutileiro Plan which recognised them as one of the entities of BH. The Muslims on the other side, after initial accepting, rejected the plan because they intended BH to be fully under Muslim control and for the Serbs to be a minority with no influence. Muslims started organising in paramilitary units of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets even though the JNA existed at that time. Since Yugoslavia had its own armed force, the Serbs responded to the mobilisation and served in that army. The leadership of Republika Srpska and the leadership of Serbia and Yugoslavia had constant quarrels in 1993 and earlier but specifically after 1994, August 1994, when all relations were suspended including even communications. The interruption of the relation proves in every way that the leadership of the Republika Srpska was not an extended arm of the authorities in Serbia. Already in April 1992, Muslims and Croats set up barricades on numerous roads in the municipality of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: My apologies for interrupting, Dr. Karadzic, but at this point it may be that some of the summary relates to part of the statement that had been removed on Your Honour's order. So just to highlight that as an observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, but, Excellency, I didn't know that it's going to be, and it is not evidence anyway. So why it couldn't be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While it is not evidence there is no need for you to continue to read that part, but please pay attention to the redaction and continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must admit it's hard for me now to be able to tell just off the cuff. I heard a moment ago, and I didn't have time to adjust things in the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break now for half an hour? Yes, we will resume at 10 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I continue in English. From the beginning of the conflict until late June, early July 1992, the Doboj Crisis Staff did not have any contact with or receive any instructions from the republican authorities in Pale, since Doboj and Teslic were the only municipalities in the entire Doboj region that remained under the control of Serbian forces and were completely cut off from the Serbian leadership. Established in May and June 1992, the Crisis Staff was created by the municipal organs because of the imminent threat of war. Its role was to supply and assist the population and organise the efficient work of the municipal organs. The Crisis Staff did not extend its powers to the police or the army and it stopped working soon after the municipality got organised. Before the signing of the Dayton Accord, Republika Srpska had a very specific military organisation. Since the Supreme Commander had to share his power with the commander of the general headquarters, since the May 12 1992, this post was held by General Mladic because of this duality of command, the relationship between Mladic and Karadzic were unbearable. At that time, the Supreme Commander did not have any role or responsibility in respect to the approving of military operations. Its only role was to discuss and resolve the army's logistical problems due to the grave material and financial situation in the army itself and Republika Srpska. Dr. Karadzic was against the military operation in Srebrenica and he expressed his concern during a Supreme Command meeting which also attended by Milan Ninkovic, and in 1993 Karadzic strongly opposed the advance of the army towards Srebrenica. They also met in order to discuss the poor functioning of the authorities in the municipality. Dr. Karadzic was concerned about the difficulty to establish the rule of law and to protect the personal safety and property of all civilians regardless of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ninkovic, since the Trial Chamber excluded a few paragraphs from the statement that have to do with Doboj for the most part, I'm going to put a few questions to you, live, in relation to that. Could you tell us, first, when the war started or, rather, when the fighting started in Doboj and who was fighting in Northern Bosnia and Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at the broader region in Posavina, Bosanski Brod, Derventa the fighting started considerably earlier, a month or two before the conflict broke out on the 3rd of May, 1992, in Doboj. The population from these areas fled to Doboj. The roads were blockaded, the approaches to Doboj, because Doboj is a big centre and roads lead in several directions from there. The fighting started on the 3rd of May because of the blockade of roads because the JNA had the deadline by which it was supposed to withdraw from these territories. That was the 19th of May, 1992. Otherwise, in Doboj, there were four military barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, to clarify, the Chamber ordered redaction of those paragraphs because it found those paragraphs not relevant. It didn't mean to tell you to lead live about those paragraphs. Mr. Robinson, I take it Mr. Karadzic understood that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I'm not asking about those paragraphs now. I want to establish something about the broader area of Northern Bosnia where some municipalities are. Actually, Brcko and others are included in the indictment. I want to see when the fighting started and who was involved in the fighting and what the influence of the civilian authorities was. For example, I could do that in this case of Doboj because out of 62 municipalities, only 20 are in the indictment, and 42 municipalities are not included, although it is claimed that there had been a system that it was the system that was spurring crimes and was involved in war in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue. But your first statement was not clear. That was the reason for my intervention. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ninkovic, so who was it who was involved in fighting in Northern Bosnia, in all these municipalities around Doboj and in Doboj itself after the 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: All the fighting in Northern Bosnia, in the so-called region of Posavina, was waged by the JNA led by Colonel Stublincevic for the most part. As far as I can remember, he was withdrawing, and Ugljevik was his ultimate destination in eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina. The fighting in Bosanska Posavina took place in Bosanski Brod, Derventa, Odzak, Modrica, Samac, and partly in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the influence of the civilian authorities over this fighting up until the 20th of May?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the position of the JNA was that civilian authorities should by no means interfere in military matters. They just asked us to take care of the wounded, also, to man the army because at that time point in time, most of the members of the army came from the Republic of Serbia, all its different parts, and this army was withdrawing and part of the army were these young conscripts, the young army as they are known. They had no experience, they were withdrawing and they had no experience in terms of warfare and defence. The objective of the army was to remove barricades. There were barricades on all sides. The de-blockade of barricades, withdrawal and handing over different towns one by one, Derventa, Brod, Odzak and others, Modrica too. All of these refugees then went towards Doboj and found refuge in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What were the plans of the civilian authorities, the Serb authorities, in these municipalities? How were the problems supposed to be resolved?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Our position, especially in Doboj, if I may say, headed by myself, was that everything should be resolved by peaceful means, for several reasons. We were a mixed community. In my town, in Doboj, the structure was as follows: The president of the national defence counsel was the president of the assembly and he was an ethnic Muslim, Ahmed Alicic [phoen], also there were meetings that were often held between the executive and the military and the Municipal Assembly. We tried to resolve problems altogether, but they became increasingly complicated because paramilitary units were formed like the Patriotic League, the HVO and the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you an intercept, an interpretation that the Croatian secret service provided, and the president of the SDS of Doboj, Vinkovic, Milan is referred to. Is there a person by that name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think there are any Vinkovics in that area, in that part of the republic. I think that that probably relates to me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which positions did you hold in the municipality on the 4th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: The 4th of April, 1992? I did not hold a single important position, if I can put it that way. I was a member of parliament, and it is true that I was cut off from my superiors; in fact, by then, we were cut off from Pale, the leadership, and so on. So, I mean, I wasn't the commander of the Crisis Staff or the president of the War Presidency, although ex officio as a member of parliament I was a member of the Crisis Staff. However, I'm not sure, because some documents say that I was and others that I wasn't a member of the War Presidency, too. May I say something else? Doboj is an exception. If we bear in mind the instructions often referred to here, instructions in critical situations, in crises, Variant B was supposed to be applied in Doboj, that says that the president of the municipal board, and that was I, should be commander of the Crisis Staff. However, we in Doboj thought, and that is what I claim to this day, that this document was not binding because this document had undergone a procedure that had not actually been adopted, signed or registered. I was not commander of the Crisis Staff, as I was supposed to be on the basis of those instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show this on the ELMO because I don't know the e-court number. The intercepts, I mean. The intercept of the Croatian secret service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read this out to us.

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Inter alia, Colonel Stublincevic when speaking to the president of the SDS of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do others see this? I cannot find it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Vinkovic, Milan is asking this one to be more involved in organising the medical service, taking in refugees and supplying food, whereas he should be allowed to carry out this operation because now, when combat starts he has to think of units, also he is asking the same person not to send small groups of people to him but, rather, at least a company. I did not mobilise people and, I mean, I did not have such powers. Secondly once in Podnovlje I met this Colonel Stublincevic, and he was speeding things up in order to withdraw from the Posavina theatre of war. As I've already mentioned, I think that his ultimate destination was Ugljevik. And then he clashed with part of the officers there, and I happened to be there, I don't know why, so I saw this quarrel and this meeting simply broke down. It almost turned into an incident. I never saw Stublincevic again, and I never sent him, I mean, any kind of groups or for me to send him a company. That makes no sense whatsoever because he had the JNA with him, the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I also have to say that this Colonel Stublincevic was not very well liked among the population because -- because of the withdrawal of the JNA he was removing barricades, and when he would do that, and when JNA units would pass there, then everything would remain the same. The Muslim-Croat forces would take the roads again, as well as the already-taken locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But what was the attitude of the SDS and the Doboj municipal authorities regarding the response to mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, our position had been known from before, and that is that the Serbian Democratic Party and the Serbian people would not establish any kind of paramilitary units or anything similar to it, but they would rather abide by the then-law on the national defence and they responded to the call-up of the JNA, and were recruited into its ranks. It is well-known that the BH territorial staff issued an order to mobilise conscripts into the Territorial Defence instead of the only legitimate armed force of the Yugoslav People's Army because just like Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was still part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, with regard to this document, Minister, can you tell us how does it fit with your experience relating to who was involved in the fighting prior to the 20th of May and how much influence the civilian structures had on the fighting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when the Yugoslav People's Army and the police force who were of mixed composition solved the problem of Doboj, which was a way of saving the Serbian people in Eastern Bosnia because 12 municipalities around Doboj had fallen into the Croatian and Muslim hands, the Yugoslav People's Army found itself under blockade in Doboj. When they removed the blockade and the roadblocks, the Yugoslav People's Army and the police -- actually they were not involved in any fighting. They practically just took over Doboj. The Muslim and Croatian forces first reached the ethnic borders and the army remained on these borders, thanks to the policy that we pursued at the time. We insisted that the JNA should not become involved and not to interfere in any regions where Serbs were not living. Doboj was divided into four municipalities on the 4th of May, and they remained as such throughout the war. And to this date, we have interethnic -- interethnicity lines and there are still four municipalities that exist in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I understand you well when you said that the Muslims and the Croats reached the -- their own ethnic boundaries and that the same boundaries remained until the end of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. They withdrew on the 3rd of May. Some of them remained but those who were armed and who were frightened because the army was adamant and issued an ultimatum for the weapons and equipment to be returned that were in the hands of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets in the part of the town called Carsija, and after that they withdrew, whereas the civilians who were unarmed remained behind. They withdrew and there is a bridge a kilometre or two from Doboj, this is where they erected a roadblock leading to Sarajevo, Teslic and so on, and they took positions on the boundaries of their villages. This was followed by provocations which prompted the Serbian forces to draw up this line which remained throughout the war until the signing of the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this intercept be admitted for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3744, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us now after the departure of the JNA, when was the Army of Republika Srpska established, and what was the influence of the civilian authorities on the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: As I already said, the army had a limited time to withdraw, and I'm talking about the JNA, and the deadline was the 19th of May, 1992. In the meantime, on the 12th of May, at the session of the National Assembly in Banja Luka, the Army of Republika Srpska was established and a number of officers and troops --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Minister, if you please give me the briefest possible answers in order to save time. So after the 12th of May and the establishment of the army, tell me who was attacking and who was defending in Doboj and what was the influence of the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: We in the civilian authorities kept insisting not to proceed further on from the ethnic boundaries established in our municipality. That was our position. And the army did not launch any attacks but, rather, put up a defensive existence -- resistance because the army wanted to defend the refugees and everything else that was situated in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A minute ago you said that civilians were against the crossing over.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D9231 in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what we see on this screen and who is the author of this book?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: What I see on the screen is a book written by Colonel Lisica who later became a general, and the title is, "The Commander Without any Need." He wrote several books and he was the commander of the Doboj operations group. After the corridor was opened, he returned to Doboj. This commander is well-known for his conflicts with the civilian authorities, and other military structures as well. In our opinion, this commander's intention by criticising the authorities was to have martial law established there. We were against that, and we tried to rein in this person and to prevent him from becoming involved in matters that were governed by the law, which is to defend the territory of our municipality and the general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page? Actually, page 2 of the document. Can we please zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And would you be kind so as to read the first ten or so lines and tell me whether this is consistent with what you have experienced?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: In the area of responsibility of the Doboj operations group, it says that the front was about 420 kilometres long, and it was stable. I can't see clearly. He says that there were several attempts to introduce radical changes on the front line in 1992 and early 1993, but it did not yield any considerable military victories but only rendered the tactical position slightly better by occupying the village Matuzici, the destructive acting of the president of the SDS Doboj was prevented, which he tried to pursue through the people who thought the same as he did in the units of the Doboj operations group. The propaganda in the units was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down because we are interpreting what is being read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read very slowly? We heard until, "The propaganda in the units was --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Propaganda in the unit was, in inverted commas, save your lives, politicians will take care of it. Active duty officers are communists, people who are interested only in careers, et cetera, unquote. The Colonel allegedly quoted my statement because he failed in his initiative. I particularly was against this operation because Matuzici village is situated in the southern part of our municipality which was divided into the Muslim and Serbian part. By occupying this municipality, we would practically encroach upon the Muslim part of the territory of the municipality, which was ethnically pure and we were opposed to that, and then he alleged that the army and some people on the opposite side realised that this was a political goal and as a result the Colonel blamed me for the failure of that offensive against this populated area where about 12.000 Muslims used to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can these two pages be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one thing to note. This document has been notified to the Prosecution but the prior document wasn't. I made no objection but just to observe that there wasn't any notification in relation to the last one and obviously this one hasn't been translated and is linked to one of the documents that you've excluded in your order related to paragraph 34, I think, of the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This was referred to in paragraph 53.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's absolutely right. Yes, yes, Mr. President. I was just referring to the same individual who is the author of the document at paragraph 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3745, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for us, by citing your personal example, the attitude towards minorities, Muslims and Croats, how many of them were in Doboj after delineation took place, and what was the attitude towards them? And I'm talking about official structures.

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: After the division of the municipal territory into four municipalities, a large number of Muslims and Croats remained in Doboj. Those who were armed withdrew and crossed over to the other side. The problem was that their families, Muslim and Croat families, remained in Doboj, whereas those fit for military service crossed over and joined their units. In fact, at least that's what people were saying, that they were shelling Doboj from the other side because it is well-known that Doboj was the town that was hit by the largest number of shells. Even after the Dayton Agreement, around 110 people were killed on the streets of the town itself, and in the area more than 1500. So our position was that everyone can remain and exercise and enjoy all their rights with regard to health care, pensions, et cetera, and as far as I know, there were no major incidents in Doboj. If there were any, this was done by specific individuals and I think that they are being prosecuted for what they did. I don't know if this answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what was the attitude towards prisoners of war captured by the JNA and later by the VRS? And from the point of view of your office as a minister, what was the position of the official authorities regarding prisoners of war throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: As I already said, there were four military barracks in Doboj. One or two of them were converted into camps but those were not camps in the standard meaning of the word. When 12 municipalities around Doboj fell, we had an influx of some 40.000 to 60.000 refugees. There were Croats who remained there were the subjects of maltreatment by the people who came from elsewhere. So the authorities established kind of reception centres to provide accommodation for those people and they used the barracks for those purposes. We also asked the International Red Cross to come over and register everyone who was there. Initially, they had to undertake work obligation but later on these camps, and as I said these were not camps in the classic sense of the word, after they were disbanded they were exchanged and went elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Minister, I have no further questions for you at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ninkovic, your evidence-in-chief has been admitted as you have noted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony in its most part. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I don't know what it was that was omitted, but very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Ninkovic, I'd like to go through your various appointments at the outset. You were an SDS deputy in the Bosnian Serb Assembly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. In the council of municipalities, the assembly had the Chamber of peoples and the Chamber of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, Mr. Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I was elected as a deputy in the Chamber of municipalities. At the time, the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina had two Chambers, the Chamber of peoples and the Chamber of municipalities. Deputies for the Chamber of municipalities were elected in the territory of only one municipality, and for me specifically that was the territory of the municipality of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: President of the SDS municipal board in Doboj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Member of the Crisis Staff in Doboj during and prior to the war, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Look, I think the Crisis Staff was formed -- I cannot remember exactly when. It wasn't formed by the organs of the Serbian Democratic Party but by organs of the Serbian municipality of Doboj, when the municipality was divided. I was the member of the Crisis Staff automatically because I was a deputy but I did not accept the post of commander of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just the translation, line 14, perhaps it would be better to say "ex officio," not "automatically." Ex officio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were employed by the Crisis Staff, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: How do you mean employed? No one was --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were a -- you were a member of the Crisis Staff. You accept that, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were one of the -- or you were the accused's recommended candidate for the position of minister of defence in the government of Dusan Kozic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have P01398 up on the screen? This is minutes of the RS Assembly's 44th session held on 18th of August, 1994, which you'll be familiar with; is that right? You'll be familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the assembly session when I was elected as minister of defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we go to page 47 of the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we stay on -- the last line in English says 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, I -- that has to be an error of transcription or translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Certainly the box further up says 18th August, 1994, and if you turn over the page to page 2, again it's repeated, the date is 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can go please to B/C/S page 31 and to the English at page 47.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now I'd like to read out to you Dr. Karadzic's commendation of you. This paragraph -- you find the paragraph that begins -- it's the top of the page for you in B/C/S. In English it's the second paragraph. "Of course the government should not look as I want it to look," that paragraph. I was looking about ten lines down in English to where it starts, "He resolutely requested," and that's talking about Dusan Kozic, have you found that in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: No. At the topic see Mr. Radovan Karadzic and then at the bottom I see Mr. Kozic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Have you got page -- you got page -- it's 31, please, of the B/C/S. Is that the page that's up? My apologies, 30 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous page, the previous in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's page 32 of the B/C/S - I do apologise - in e-court. So there we are. That's -- the paragraph begins, "Of course the government should," and if you can go down about three or four sentences to where it starts "He resolutely requested," got that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: I still don't have that page. I'm looking at page 31.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's the right page. At the top of the page it should say something to the effect of course the government should not look as I want it to look. Is that right? Is that what it says? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I don't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can you read from the top of the page, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: It is page 31.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Just that page, would you read it, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's very small, and it's a bit too far. Of course, the government should not look as I -- it's very small, the letters are too small. The way I want it to look, and it doesn't look as I want it. It has to look the way Kozic wants it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay, that's the right paragraph. Thank you. Now I'm going to take up further down a couple of sentences down where it starts - it goes as follows: "He resolutely requested that a member of the Main Staff should be the Defence Minister and that is where I was persistent, with all due respect, to the people from the Main Staff," and then it goes over to page 48 in the English, same page B/C/S, "to the Main Staff who were mentioned but the position of the Main Board is that it has to be a civilian because the Main Staff has a very prominent and outstanding person heading it, General Mladic.
