Anyone who would become minister would have to salute General Mladic while the minister should be someone who is the master in that field." And it goes on: "I'll take it up here. I must say that I've heard different things about Ninkovic. I've heard that in Doboj he has things under his control to such an extent that we have lost some people due to that. They went over to the radicals. They say it is because Ninkovic has everything under his control. It was an argument in his favour rather than one against him, because if he can control a huge municipality while he is not even its president, he can influence the events. It gave me some hope that it is possible for him to introduce order in the army as well." Now, here is the question. You've testified today that you didn't hold a single important position in Doboj. That was your testimony, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I did have a position, the position of party president, until March 1992, when the premises of the Serbian Democratic Party were bombed and because of many barricades at the approaches to Doboj and because of the general political situation. We suspended the work of the party until further notice, and because of that I did not have any more positions other than the one of member of the Crisis Staff. I'm talking about 1992. As for this here, as far as I can remember, the assembly meeting at which I was elected minister was also attended by my predecessors, ministers from the officer cadre, and their position was that they had lower ranks than that of the commander of the Main Staff, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the content of that meeting, the assembly meeting. Please wait a moment. I'm asking you about your position in Doboj. Now, you testified this morning that you didn't hold a single important position in Doboj. And my question to you is: The fact of the matter is you controlled the municipality, right, during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. How could I control the municipality? The municipality was controlled by the Crisis Staff, headed by the commander of the Crisis Staff. The municipality was controlled by the civilian structures, by the name of War Presidency, and these two institutions functioned for a very short period of time, as soon as there were conditions created so that the assembly, Municipal Assembly, could meet and the Executive Board could meet, the Crisis Staff stopped operating. I said that I was a member of the Crisis Staff, but I was not the person at its head.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm not talking about who is head of the Crisis Staff. I'm talking about what Radovan Karadzic says here which is appointments or not he controlled the municipality. Is that a -- a statement that is not accurate, so far as you're concerned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: I was the president of the winning party in Doboj, and, of course, I dealt with the setting up of the government until the work of the party was frozen in March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to go to another exhibit, please. Can we have 65 ter 12084.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You had spoken earlier about the 1991 instructions which you said, what, they weren't binding? You didn't follow them? What's your position? Stop -- answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What -- what question? I didn't understand the question. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: My question is did you follow the 1991 instructions in Doboj. Just answer the question. Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: We did not. We did not because the instruction said one thing and we did another thing. If you have the instruction so that you can look on the page towards the bottom of the page, the commander of the Crisis Staff should be the president of the municipal board of the Serbian Democratic Party and that was not the case in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Just look at the article at the bottom of the page, please. It's an interview with you in "Novo Glas" dated 26th of March, 1993. Got it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That is, isn't it, the anniversary of the setting up in Doboj of the Serbian municipality, the various Serbian institutions that were set up on the 26th of March, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Here you are in an article and you can see how that article is headed, Milan Ninkovic, president of --

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Took over.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: President of the SDS in Doboj and a member of parliament, we assumed historical responsibility. And it says, on the eve of the anniversary of the formation of the Serbian municipality in Doboj, the place and role of the SDS both on the level of Republika Srpska and Doboj municipality must be recognised. Mr. Milan Ninkovic, president of the municipal board of the SDS Doboj and a member of parliament, is the most competent person to present its evaluation. Now if we could just turn in the English, please, to the second pain of page and I'd like you to look in the B/C/S, please, at --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness have the original version considerably magnified, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, I'd agree. Let me just identify the paragraph which needs to be magnified for the witness. It's the third paragraph. So it's -- it's the middle paragraph -- it's a bit unfortunate actually because it's -- it straddles all three columns.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can you -- can you see it now, Mr. Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: I see it but I cannot read it. Somebody can read it. I don't know if it's my glasses or something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well the first paragraph I'm not going to deal with. So we are going to the third paragraph where it starts: "It is a general opinion that the SDS has successfully ended the first period of work in which we gathered all the Serbs?" Can you see where that starts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: I see it, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd like to read the rest out. Could you read it out loud, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well: "Back in December 1991, according to precise and strict instructions of the Main Board of the party, OOSDS Doboj formed a secretariat of the party, formed a Crisis Staff and issued a decision on the initiation of preparations for the formation of the Serbian Municipality of Doboj, constitution of its assembly and relevant organs. Through different forms of organising, the SDS tried to express the political interests of the Serbian people because its representatives are in the assembly, government and Presidency, and were literally pushed out by outvoting and a coalition of the SDA and the HDZ representatives. After the famous events in March and April 1992, the party assumed the historical responsibility of organising the prevention of a new genocide.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So there we are. You followed the precise and strict instructions of the SDS Main Board, that is the December 1991 instructions, is that correct, looking at this now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But there is a problem there. The formation of Serbian municipalities was a response to a different question. If you permit me, I can clarify that a little bit. Serbs always responded to a given situation. What we would say an action -- a reaction in response to an action, starting in October 1992 and then things went on from there. The Croat-Muslim coalition would make one move and we would respond to that move. That's how things proceeded. And then when this decision was made to go to a referendum on the 28th of February and the 1st of March, 1991, without the Serbs, our response was to form Serbian entities, autonomous provinces, Serbian municipalities, from local communes up to the largest entities, and that's how in Doboj the Serbian Municipality of Doboj was formed, and then on the other side also the Muslim municipality of Doboj, Doboj east, was formed. And what I'm saying is --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm asking you a question about the 1991 instructions. Now, the question is: Whether or not what you state here in this article in terms back in December 1991, according to the precise and strict instructions of the Main Board of the party, the OOSDS Doboj formed a secretariat, formed a Crisis Staff and issued a decision on initiation of preparations and so on. Did you follow in Doboj the precise and strict instructions, as is said here, that were contained in the 1991 December instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we be more specific, please? Does the Prosecutor mean the paper known as A and B, or some other instruction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your intervention is not appropriate. Her question is based on this article.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Your objection is overruled. Please answer the question, Mr. Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's true that in 1991 the secretariat was formed, the secretariat was formed as the inner executive body of the municipal board. That is correct. But now, the Crisis Staff was not formed in 1991. I told you that the Crisis Staff was formed by the Serbian municipality that was formed on the 26th of March, 1991. Actually, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Break it up. Let's break it up. Let's break my question up. Back in December 1991, did you follow the precise and strict instructions, the precise and strict instructions, of the SDS Main Board as you state here in the article?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not. I would like to explain. The secretariat was formed. I don't know if the instructions envisaged the formation of secretariats. The municipality was formed after the 28th of February and the 1st of March when independence was voted and when the referendum was held among the other two peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the 26th of March - on the 26th of March, I say again - the Serbian Municipality of Doboj was formed because it was formed because of the inability to meet, then the Crisis Staff was formed, and then, on the 26th of March, the party suspended its work. Of course, we did take part in it. We just said that we from the Serbian Democratic Party suspended our work. We cannot form a Crisis Staff. This is something that would be done by the municipalities. The practice for the Crisis Staff was that they had plans but the implementation of those plans depended on the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The instructions, we are talking about the 1991 instructions, they call for a party secretariat, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. The secretariat is the operative body of the municipal board because the municipal board had problems to meet, so that everything could be regular, then the secretariat was formed, which is actually a kind of executive body of the municipal board.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff in Doboj co-ordinated -- co-ordinated the military and civilian authority, didn't it, in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know in what sense it was standing by its army and it took care mostly of refugees. You need to view Doboj in a special context. As I said, 12 municipalities around Doboj fell into enemy hands and the refugees arrived, and they couldn't go anywhere from Doboj. The entire region, which had eight or nine municipalities, only two municipalities, that of Doboj and Teslic, stayed in Serbian hands, i.e., under Serbian rule. So the Crisis Staff was mostly dealing with these problems, trying to calm the situation down.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let me just -- let me just focus -- focus your answer, I focus the question. You in the Crisis Staff made the decision to attack and take over Doboj, right, and the army acted on that decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] I'm going to ask you to look at another document, please. It's 65 ter 25274, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit the document, 12084.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I would be grateful, yes. I -- I -- I would ask to admit that document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6418, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before we proceed further, when was it then you were appointed as minister of defence, Mr. Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 18th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I remember Mr. Karadzic you in reading out the summary, you introduced that he was appointed as minister of defence after the war. Where is it -- where in the statement does it dealt it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Towards the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It is the case that he was reappointed to that position after the war, Mr. President, if that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could clarify with the witness. So you were appointed in 1994 and continued to be the minister of defence after the war, or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I can -- can help you with the dates, Mr. Ninkovic, if it would help. You were appointed Mr. Dusan Kostic's [sic] government on 18th of August, 1994, then again to that position, to the position of minister of defence in --

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Kozic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Vojko Kazicic's [phoen] on the 17th of December, 1995, and then again in 1996 to the following government in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: And then one more time in the government after that, in four governments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The government of Dusan Kozic, the government of Kasagic and twice the government of Klickovic. That's how it should have been stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not knowing the names of the governments, I'm not sure whether the witness continued to be the minister of defence or there were intervals. Could you clarify with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's all the way through, isn't it? You were reappointed all the way through from August 1994, then again in December 1995, then in May 1996, and again in November 1996 and that was a continual in effect reappointment over that period; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Governments changed, and Minister Ninkovic remained in each and every one of the coming governments.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President could we move on to the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's up now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, here is a broadcast and I'm going to take you to a very limited number of lines in this broadcast. You can see there the title, it's the record of the Serbian Radio Doboj programme broadcast on the 2nd of May, 1997, to mark the fifth anniversary of the forcible takeover of government in the town of Doboj. And you are amongst the guests during that broadcast; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Where does it say forcible takeover of government? I cannot see that. You must added that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I haven't added anything. If you look at the heading, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's an article that you have confirmed [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I do apologise, I just don't know who wrote the heading. It certainly wasn't the editor who was conducting the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well let's move on from the heading. Let's go to page 2, please, of the English, and in the B/C/S, please, page 2 as well. And I want to take you to Joganovic's [phoen] question which you can just see at the bottom towards the bottom in the B/C/S. It says, "The army was by definition an extended hand of politics." "When was the political decision made to take control of the town," Mr. Agoian [phoen] said referring to an earlier answer. And then you take on the answer to this question, you say, "This must be a question for me. It is true we were organised in this way." I'm not going to read the whole paragraph. Let me just take it up from about halfway -- about six lines down you said: "Because according to the instruction we received from above everyone had the right, in other words everyone had to do their job. I was in charge of Doboj municipality but I was not allowed and our organisation for instance to get involved and help Maglaj municipality," and then you go on. There again you're stating that you were in charge of Doboj; is that accurate? Does that accurately describe the position you held over the municipality of Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the organs of the party at republican level. Of course, as member of parliament elected by that same people, I was supposed to take care of the people from that point of view. We had constant problems with the military in Doboj. We had problems with the army in Doboj then as well. We wanted things to be resolved by peaceful means but they said that they could not wait for that, that they had to resolve that in a different way, in a military way. However, when the telegram arrived from Sarajevo, from the Territorial Defence, to the effect that Doboj should be taken by the Patriotic League and the rest, and bearing in mind that all other municipalities in that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina had fallen, then the army decided that and we did not oppose it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You're moving on from what I directly asked you on to other matters. What I directly asked you is whether you were in charge of Doboj and you now accept that, do you? You accept you were in charge and in control of Doboj municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what sense you mean, that I was in charge. How could I exercise control over the Crisis Staff when they have a leadership of their own? How can I exercise control over the Serb municipality when I do not head that Serb municipality and so on? The party had frozen its work and we had political influence but we did not decide on anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Ninkovic, these are your words. These are your words.

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. But you have to bear in mind that this is some kind of an anniversary, and then for political reasons, well, you know, elections are getting closer, so I allow for that possibility that I did say some of that, but I'm saying what the situation was. Do you understand that? These political speeches and political statements cannot always be taken at face value.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay, let's look at a document that isn't an article.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to admit in evidence just the portion upon which I've relied, which is as described it's at page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit it as Exhibit P6419.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, may we admit the entire article? There is another aspect that would be useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary, Mr. Karadzic may lead that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to 65 ter 11270, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You maintain in your evidence that the rights of the non-Serbian population in Doboj were maintained and upheld, is that right, during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to go into this to show you this document. Let's move, please, in the English to page 4 and in the B/C/S to page 3. Now, these are two decisions I'm going to ask you to look at. The first decision is a decision by the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Doboj - and I'll show you the end of the document in a moment - dated the 24th of June, 1992, and it's addressed to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Ministry of Justice. You can see that. And if we just turn to page 2 of the English, you can stay where we are in the B/C/S -- I mean, sorry, page 5 of the English. Now we can see what this decision is about. It is a decision which proposes to the Ministry of Justice the removal -- you can see it on your page -- the removal of non-Serbs from judicial positions citing a decision of the ARK Crisis Staff that only Serbs can have leading positions in state institutions. And you can see in the handwriting, you can see the names of three non-Serbs identified, whose -- who are to be removed from their positions and you can see handwritten relieved next to their names, can't you? And I would say -- just point you to the top of the page, you can see some handwriting at the top of the page in the B/C/S and it's actually the preceding page 4 in the English. It says handwritten done, yes? And there are some Serbian prosecutors identified to replace the non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, you can see that. Can you -- can you just confirm that you can see the document, it's clearly there for you? Yes? You would have been aware of decisions of this nature?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, first of all I have to correct you. You said Crisis Staff. The Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serb Municipality of Doboj, signed president. This has nothing to do with the Crisis Staff. So this is the Serb municipality of Doboj, and if you go further down, you will see it says president, and when you spoke, you said that it was the Crisis Staff that had proposed this. This is --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Are you trying to say you have nothing to do with this because it's not the Crisis Staff, it's just the president; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. The Crisis Staff and the Serb municipality is not the same thing. You said the Crisis Staff proposes judges. That's not true. The organ in charge is called the Serb municipality of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Show the bottom of the page in B/C/S, please, and you can see, please, in the English at page 6, you see the stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, while we are still here, please, take a look at the translation for "predlazimo," "we wish to nominate," "recommend" is one thing, "nominate" is another thing. [In English] "The area of judiciary and Prosecution, we wish to nominate." [Interpretation] "To appoint," and the original says, "we propose." And then of course, it is left to the minister to decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, can we -- can we -- can we please go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the end of what Mr. Karadzic stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please do not overlap -- [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we zoom in to the stamp? Just the stamp, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You can see that, can't you, that that's a stamp which has I said on it the assembly of Serbian municipality of Doboj Crisis Staff, at least that's how it's translated. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina, no. The assembly of the Serb municipality of Doboj, and in very small letters, very fine print, it says "Crisis Staff." You see here it says "the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," then the "assembly of the Serb municipality of Doboj," big letters, and then in the middle it says "Crisis Staff." And you see in the heading of the document, it says it's the "Serb municipality of Doboj." I don't know what the Crisis Staff had to do with it because it wasn't functioning at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's -- let's leave that. This is a document then with a proposal for the removal of three non-Serbs from this position, a recommendation for the appointment of three Serbian prosecutors. And let us, please, go to the second page in the English, and in the B/C/S, please, let us go to similarly the second page. This is a decision -- can't see it in the English but in the B/C/S you can see it all. It's a decision, isn't it, by which Radovan Karadzic appoints the Serbian candidates to the positions that we've spoken about, isn't it? Do you agree? In the English if we just look at page 3. You can see there the signatory and the date.

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That can be seen, but I cannot see here in the heading on the basis of such and such article of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I cannot clarify that, the decision is correct, and then from the previous document you can see that the persons who were proposed were accepted and they were appointed to these positions of senior public attorney in Doboj, and so on and so forth, Stokic, Zoran, I don't know, whatever all their names were. You cannot really see it here. Panic Dusko, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We don't need to go -- we can see the document it -- it -- it identifies these same persons.

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to have that document admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, I do not see on the basis of which article the president made these appointments up here, on the basis of which legal documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, may that document be admitted in evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6420, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let's move on to 1995. Now, you were in Western Bosnia during the Srebrenica preparations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say exactly, but from time to time I came to the headquarters in Pale by helicopter and then I'd return and so on. As for supplies, I was transferred to the western part of the front line to bring together the operation of the 11 municipalities that were undergoing a crisis, that were attacked from all sides. It was necessary to organise civilian life. Also manning, material supplies as well. So with General Milovanovic and the Minister of Justice, I was in the western part of the front when Muslim and Croat forces attacked the western part of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I want to ask you about Srebrenica. Now you talk in your statement about a meeting you had with Radovan Karadzic, the meeting on the 18th of July and also 26th of July. Is that when you had returned full time from Western Bosnia or did you just drop in for those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that it just so happened that I was there. I cannot recall the subject that we discussed. However, there is the name of a particular person there, Maksim Stanisic, who was president of the Executive Board, the head of the executive government of Sarajevo, and there were some problems in that part of Sarajevo so that's probably what we discussed. I think that at that meeting there was no discussion concerning Srebrenica. Had that happened, I certainly would have remembered it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: When were you debriefed then about the involvement of your ministry in removing elderly men, women and children from the Srebrenica area, from Potocari? When were you -- when were you debriefed about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand you. What do you mean, what ministry? It's not the ministry that carried out the removal of civilians from Srebrenica. The ministry played a completely different role in that homeland war of ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: What does the ministry have to do with Srebrenica, except for certain things that at the request of the Main Staff, certain buses and trucks, et cetera, were mobilised and placed at the disposal of the Main Staff. That's the only role of the ministry in the operation that was in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: When were you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, before you go further, let me put this question to the witness: Mr. Karadzic was the Supreme Commander in his capacity of the president; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And General Mladic was the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you were the member of the Supreme Command in the capacity of minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you explain to us the relation amongst these three individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have said earlier on that I was appointed in 1994 as the first civilian minister of defence because there were major problems between the civilian authorities and the military structures, because beforehand there were two ministers who were lower-ranking officers in relation to the commander of the Main Staff. When I arrived, my task was to normalise these relations between the civilian structures and the military structures. The army was just supposed to have command responsibility over the army and all the rest should belong to the Ministry of Defence, in the following sense: Product specific production, logistics, and many other things that we often discussed, and even on an ideological and political basis, the military interfered in that and we did not allow that. I don't know if I've given a full answer, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Put it in simple terms, would it be correct that you could be regarded as superior to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In a command sense, no, but as for the rest, logistics, supplies and the rest, yes, the ministry was responsible for that. But the ministry in the situation of war, imminent threat of war, it did not have anything to do with command, just like the Supreme Command did not make decisions on any kind of operations, et cetera. It was more of an advisory body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After the war, at some point in time, the Main Staff of the VRS was transformed into a form of General Staff? Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In 1994, when I became minister, I intervened immediately in certain ways because foreign observers and some people from IFOR then had suggested to the minister of defence that this duality of command had to be resolved. However, in this constellation of relations because war operations were going on, we did not change the Law on the Army or the Law on National Defence. However, in 1996, when President Karadzic handed over his duties to Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, then we decided together to make this cut in the army and to change the Law on the Army and the Law on Defence. The essence of this change of the law was inter alia that instead of a Main Staff, the army should be headed by a General Staff, and the General Staff would be headed by the chief of General Staff, not a commander, because this is a well-known organisation of the military in all countries. The Supreme Commander, along with the Supreme Command, and then the chief of General Staff or perhaps it's called a different name in other countries, but in Yugoslavia and in Serbia and to this day in Bosnia-Herzegovina, too, there is this chief of General Staff. That's where we clashed, especially I with General Mladic, because he disagreed with that. However, we even joked a bit, that Tito in 1941 did not recognise the king as the Supreme Commander and then he was commander too, and the king was in exile in England.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So at that time, when that transformation took place, could the minister of defence be regarded as the -- as a superior to the Chief of Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no. Actually, the army was in the ministry then but we had two completely separate functions. His superior was the president of the republic as the Supreme Commander, that is to the Chief of the General Staff. And most importantly then, we managed to get the military industry out of the control of the army and this was reflected on something different later, and then Biljana returned it to the army and then these well-known dealings with Iraq and then the replacement of the president of the republic, because Orao was within the military, not the civilian structures, and they were the ones that overhauled planes for Iraq that was under international sanctions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Given the time, shall we continue after the break, Ms. Pack, if it is not inconvenient for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We touched briefly before the break on the role of the Ministry of Defence in mobilising and placing at the disposal of the Main Staff the buses, for the remove of the civilian population that had been in Srebrenica. So when were you made aware of the Ministry of Defence's contribution to this process?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember exactly, bearing in mind that I was in the western part of Republika Srpska. Upon arrival at the ministry, I had an assistant who was in charge of mobilisation, but he deferred this at a lower level of the secretariat, and then further down to ministry departments and then the departmental allocate this to various municipalities pursuant to the request of the Main Staff. But as I said, I cannot tell you the exact time when I learned about the mobilisation of assets and this is actually standard procedure applied in the ministry. When we requisition or mobilise vehicles or similar assets we do not inquire to what purposes these assets are needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This wasn't a standard operation, was it? It was a huge operation. Now I'm asking you approximately, approximately when -- can you recall what month, when -- when can you recall you were told about this significant contribution that was made by your ministry?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, look, my assistant for mobilisation of assets was in charge of that and he forwarded that to lower level so that's three steps downwards, and even four steps downwards from me. Now, when was it that I learned about this and when I returned, I don't know. I heard about the operation of Srebrenica in -- on TV. We were in Drvar and that is when I heard that the operation Srebrenica was successfully completed military operation. And that was all that was broadcast and carried in the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can you remember roughly when you came back, what time of year, what time of year were you debriefed about your ministry's role?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot -- I cannot remember when I returned from the western front. My assistant didn't need to inform me about this because when they were doing other sorts of mobilisations, they had never informed me about that. For example, when they were mobilising manpower, conscripts, people for work obligation, they never informed me on that as well, because as I said that was a standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Are you saying now that you weren't informed about this -- these mobilisations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: At one point you became aware, did you, that there had been a remove from the Srebrenica area, from Potocari, thousands of men, children, elderly men, women and children, in buses, some of which had been mobilised by the Ministry of Defence; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the Ministry of Defence that mobilised the buses, the order signed by my assistants, I saw that for the first time during my testimony before The Hague Tribunal, and it was only recently that I saw these order because whenever I returned from some trip, I never wanted and asked them to see every single order that were sent downwards to the level of municipalities, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's your evidence that the first time you heard about your ministry's involvement in the mobilisation of buses was before you testified here in these proceedings? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I saw these orders, four or five of them, for the first time before I came to testify here because when I returned to the ministry, I did not request my assistants to show me the orders that they had issued. And for your information, there are ministry departments, there are secretariats, which comprise several ministries, there is an assistant minister for mobilisation, and finally on the top of the pyramid there is the minister which means there are four levels.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You learned of course that the civilian population were removed from the Srebrenica area, you learned that many years ago, you're not saying that this is something that was also newly learnt on your arrival here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not what I said. I found out about this from the media during and after the operation itself, because it was shown on TV that buses and lorries were leaving for Tuzla and Kladanj and other places where the populations were being relocated to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I realise my time is up. I have no further questions for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pack. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Minister, let us start from the last question and your answer to it. It has been suggested to you, and interpreted to you, that these civilians were removed, whereas you said that they were relocated. Did you have any information about them having been removed in terms of forcible relocation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was mention of some disagreements with the army. As for the Army of Republika Srpska as a state organ, had they committed any crime that you as a minister should have known about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the army did not commit any crimes. I am convinced of that, being a member of the Supreme Command and knowing you, had we found out that the army had committed any kind of crimes, and bearing in mind the tensions that existed between the military, the Supreme Command and the civilian authorities, I am convinced, and I am sure that you would have dismissed immediately some people primarily General Mladic, the Chief of the General Staff, because we could hardly wait for something to pin on him because our option, and your option, was to try and solve everything in a peaceful manner, and we kept insisting at all meetings of the government and the assembly that the peace plan is the priority and that they should only defend the reached separation lines. You were always against any other kind of action and you always advocated a peaceful end to the war, just like every war has to end with a peace agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber if there -- or our crimes were not the reason for the tensions with the army, what was the underlying reason for these disagreements?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: I said in my statement, I don't know if that was accepted, the reasons were such as the supplies for the army. One part of the army wanted to provide their own supplies. We place under the civilian control and the government control some of the facilities of the military-industrial complex, then there was the issue of promotion of officers, and many other things such as the system of disseminating information, et cetera, et cetera. All of these things existed until the Dayton Accords, when the army became an integral part of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On pages 58 and 59, you were shown document P6420, which relates to the dismissal of three individuals from the judiciary. Those were presumably three Muslims or three non-Serbs. Can you tell us what was the most common reason for dismissals in our country before that time, during that time, and afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, but the people who used to work in those institutions did not wish to continue working there because, for example, in the judiciary, there were no trials of Muslims and Croats because they had already left. Most of those who were tried were Serbs and, of course, it is only natural that you have Serbs working in those institutions. That was a general attitude. But later on, this slowly became more balanced. For example, in the MUP, there were many people of other ethnicities and there were mixed marriages. However, judiciary is a rather sensitive area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As for the remaining three municipalities of Doboj, one Croatian and two Muslim ones were there any police stations and who worked there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. Before the creation of the Serbian municipality of Doboj there had already been some ideas and plans in order how to divide Doboj. When the clashes started, they divided the municipality and their Crisis Staff existed before ours. These three municipalities, because the municipality of Doboj Usora is a smaller one and part of it belonged to us, although it was populated by Croats; in other words, they established parallel institutions as we did, and at certain periods they even conducted negotiations on how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the two Muslim municipalities of Doboj were there any Serb policemen just like there were Muslim policemen in the Serbian municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: That was out of the question, and the situation remains the same to this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Objection. Mr. President, I've not objected to the prior two questions. I've let them go, but it may be that we are straying on to an area which is going into the specifics and details in matters in Doboj municipality which I didn't question the witness on. I did -- I did question him about [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he's a moving on. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies, with a question pertained to the reasons for dismissals, that's what I wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me for how many days could one be absent from work without being dismissed, and after which period a dismissal was inevitable?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I really cannot remember. It is in the domain of administrative procedures, and I am not versed in that area because that was something done by the lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time, can you tell us, if you know, if I appointed any Muslims and Croats in the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I really cannot remember. If somebody would help me in order to remind me, I might be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have this in the evidence so I will drop it. On page 50, you were asked about the instructions received from the party. Were there any instructions issued by the party apart from the well known A and B variants? Was that the only instruction, or did the party send any other instructions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, bearing in mind that the communications channels were severed, I think that this was distributed, this instruction was distributed at the Holiday Inn without any prior debate. We all received it, it was handed out to each and every one of us, but it was not the subject of any discussion and we just took it with us to our respective grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before the war, did the party issue any proclamations and send them out to their municipal boards before the communications were severed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean exactly. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Minister, in the question on page 50, it was not said precisely that it was document A and B. So I'm asking you, apart from document A and B, was there any other document -- communication with the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Not that I can remember, on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I didn't mean on that basis but we shall leave this subject. You said that the situation in Doboj was such that it was moving towards a peaceful solution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now have 1D9235 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, this hasn't been notified. I don't know why it's being produced in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are not obligated to notify documents in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As long as it arises from the line of cross. But do you not notify the Prosecution at the beginning of the re-examination? I don't know the practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 29th of April, which means two or three days before the events in Doboj. Please read lines 6 and 7, which reads, "According to his statement ...," can you find it? There is the mention of 300 fighters and then the mention of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "According to his statement, the situation in Doboj is peaceful and it is being pursued in order to achieve a peaceful option." Look, we had a very specific situation. As I said before, all the other municipalities were in their hands and there was fighting in Posavina, then the operation in Posavina spilled over only 11 kilometres from the centre of the town in the places of Kotorsko and Orahovac, and it even involved regular Croatian forces. As a result, we held a series of meetings with our adversaries at the village of Seslije in order to agree not to launch any attacks on Doboj municipality because the distance from the north or -- and from the south was about 50 kilometres so Doboj was in a kind of sandwich. And we were pushing the JNA to go as far away from Doboj as possible but it had already been blocked on those major roads that led towards Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is recorded in this intercept, is it consistent with what you know, with your experience, and was it true that actually on the 29th of April, everybody was seeking a peaceful solution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because the council for National Defence, headed by a Muslim, invited all the presidents of the municipalities, the chief of SJBs and party leaders to reach an agreement and to undertake some other actions. For example, to establish mixed military patrols, consisting of the army, the Muslims and the Croats, in order to calm down the situation. This council, led by a Muslim, insisted that the Muslims remove the roadblocks in Doboj in order to not to cause what they had already caused earlier by keeping these roadblocks in place. There is even a written document which was actually the last warning that the barricades should be removed in a peaceful way, and normal life restored.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Minister.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this intercept be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D3746, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have P6419? That was admitted into evidence a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Minister, who had power on the 1st of April, on the 1st of May, and the 1st of June in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: The 1st of April and the 1st of May 1992? Yes. Three parties had power. In 1990, the Serbian Democratic Party won the elections in Doboj, and when it came to the division of power, we had a prerogative of choosing between two places, either the president of the municipality or the president of the Executive Committee. Since it was up to me to decide, I reached an agreement with the Party of Democratic Action to offer them the post of the president of Municipal Assembly and that the Serbs should retain the post of the president of Executive Committee. And that is what we did. We had good co-operation, we had made concessions to one another, and we were friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who did you take that place of the president of the Executive Board for? Was it for yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not take it for myself. I took it for a well known person named Borislav Paravac who would later be the head of the Crisis Staff and who was also the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina after the Dayton peace accords. He was not a member of the Serbian Democratic Party. Allegedly I heard that he actually joined the party in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the 7th line what was omitted was that he was a non-party person. Could you now pay attention to this first page. According to the heading, what do you think, who made the compilation of this radio programme?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea. The Prosecution mentioned my statement. However, there is also the statement here by -- of an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army who explained what was going on in more detail here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you take over power over the Muslim and the Croat parts of the Doboj municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. In the decision of the Serbian Municipality of Doboj, that is to say in the document, it says that the municipality encompasses places where there is a majority Serbian population. No village with a majority Muslim or Croat population became part of the Serbian municipality. Pursuant to Dayton many villages and inhabited places were assigned to the municipality of Doboj, which during the war were not part of the Serbian Municipality of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paravac mentions this council that you referred to comprising Alicic and some others. There is talk about barricades. Can we look at page 2? And on the first page we can see -- can we see the bottom, Jovanovic, who is Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Security officer of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at page 2? And Jovanovic continues. At the time, on the 29th of April, when the peaceful option was embarked upon -- can you please tell us, look at "Najme" [phoen]. This is the 15th line from the bottom --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters need time to find the text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just wait till the interpreters could find the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Najme smo, smo" [phoen] is at the end. From what you can see, it's the 10th line at the end of the row.

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, we received information that in Doboj and that's where that line is. 10th line from the top, barbecue barricades, "rostilj barikade."

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: At one point we received information that they were preparing a sort of barbecue barricade which was quite a jocular manner and game of the Muslim political leadership specifically [indiscernible] we received information that a barbecue barricade was to be organised in the town of Doboj to which people would come by vehicles from Klokotnica, Brijesnica, Gracanica, Grapska, Kotorsko, and these other villages, and then these other places which at some point in time the people there would bring out their weapons and begin to occupy the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you hear when the JNA intelligence officer said that in this radio programme?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but he was an intelligence officer of the JNA who knew all of that and more, and they concealed many things from us, that is something that is known broadly, including this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at the end of this paragraph? I'm going to read it. It says: "And what Mr. Paravac said, the continuity of government was established without violence."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat his question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. Interpreters didn't hear your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: Was there a takeover of power or was there a continuity of power, as it is stated here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: The government remained the same, only the information was issued that day that the berets were being disarmed and the Patriotic League, first of all, and that everybody should remain calm and that everyone should return to their work, and so on and so forth. Nobody drove anybody out from work or anything like that. However, within a short period of time, one by one of those officials of -- from the other ethnic groups would be leaving their duties, there are some who did not leave, who stayed, to continued to carry on their work until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now please pay attention to the bottom? If we can raise and magnify this, where you speak my name, "I am a man of such a nature, I never went to sit with Radovan." Could you read a little bit and just tell us whether this is true? Could you please read it out loudly?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask for a reference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I think it's second or third line in, Ninkovic. Could you start reading again very slowly, Mr. Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you can read the second sentence, "I must say."

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: "I must say that our political leadership at the time was constantly expressing some doubts. I mean, I am by nature the kind of man, I would never go to sit with Radovan, our president, to tell him stories, to lie to him, to make promises and so on. On the occasions when I was present at these meetings, I just said everything would be okay and all right in Doboj."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct what you said in this interview?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I'm not the sort of man who wails and moans and cries, and so on and so forth. I even felt that we should resolve this in a peaceful manner, but once we split up, I did not permit the conflict to expand, as far as I was able to, but I must use this opportunity that Doboj was the town who was the most heavily bombarded town in Republika Srpska. This is why we did not move those lines. But there were ambitions constantly by the other side to capture Doboj which was a major problem in Dayton as well, when the decision was being made where that will be and how that will look.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And because of that position of yours, were you criticised by me or was that something that was to your credit; in other words, you were a minister under how many presidents? Was it just under me?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: No. When you handed over your duties to Madam Biljana Plavsic, then a government, there was a change of government, and I wanted to leave that government, the future government, and I did not wish to be nominated because the president of the republic decided about the minister of defence and minister of the interior, I think, so I asked Mrs. Biljana not to nominate me to the prime minister-designate, and not to suggest that I continue as minister at the Ministry of Defence; however, she said that the problem with the army was still not resolved and that it would be a good thing for me to stay on and that I was a reliable associate as far as she was concerned and then later she changed her mind and then presented a different story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see, it's in English, can we look at the following page? In the Serbian it's 4, and I believe -- and in English it should be one more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, here you're talking with Jorganovic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: Journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. And now, can you -- this, yes, from a part of the Serbs, can you retell what is there or can you read two of your answers and one of his? This one and the next two small ones.

utterances.speaker: MILAN NINKOVIC
utterances.text: I think the decision was not uncovered in any elements. He asked me earlier about a large number of Serbs, Muslims and Croats, in view of the fact that there were the May-day holidays, had moved out from Doboj, going out on picnics, and so on, and this happened on the 3rd of May which was not a workday. Many of them did not return to Doboj, not the Serbs, not the Muslims, not the Croats. Most probably in that sense I wanted to -- so I don't know. I said they left in -- they stayed in Usora, Tesanj, Maglaj, and other places which were still not caught by war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender these three pages that we have just looked at. Can they be added either to that one or a new number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we add page 4 to the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, and this first one, the previous one that we presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think page 1 and 2 were admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is so. Then it's just 4. We can do more. Did not say [in English] "We can do more." The page 4 is added. I'm waiting whether I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that has been added, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I'm waiting for you to direct me to go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please go on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Minister, for your service as minister and thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank you, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ninkovic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please call your next witness, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the next witness is Mirko Trivic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The associated exhibit for the next witness, his statement seems to be his diary, part of his diary. I take it you are tendering only the page, i.e. page 28, that was discussed in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Pack, would it be you that will deal with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes. It is, yes, and I have no objection to the admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that the date does not appear on this page, would the parties agree that it is related to a certain date?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, and it would perhaps be sensible to take it from an earlier page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 12th of July, 1995. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness -- oh, yes, take your time, please. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trivic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel Trivic.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you, and you can also warn me yourself, so that we both remember to speak out our sentences slowly and that between your and my replies, we break so that we have the interpretation, and when the translation is going on, I ask you to stop and then continue when it's finished so that we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will do my best to take proper part in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, sir, did you give my Defence team one statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did provide a statement to your Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D9680 in e-court, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the left side of the screen? Do you see that statement there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Let me just change my glasses. Yes, I see, on the left side of the screen, in Serbian, the beginning of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I read it and signed it, in my own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could the witness please see the last page so that he could identify his signature? Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: It is fully in line with what I had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers basically be the same as those contained in this statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The answers would basically be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender this statement in accordance with Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit the statement as well as the associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement will be Exhibit D3747 and 65 ter 25028 will be Exhibit D3748.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out the summary of Colonel Mirko Trivic's statement in the English language. [In English] Colonel Mirko Trivic served in the JNA and VRS from 1971 until 2002. In 1991, he served at the land army military academy in Belgrade. He followed the war in Slovenia and Croatia through various sources of information. Military sources from the war-torn areas were direct participants of these areas and flooded into Belgrade garrison buildings. Most of the sources of information about the real state of affairs in BH arrived in May 1992. Mirko Trivic gained personal experience being engaged in a team formed by the JNA Main Staff operations administration. Following the withdrawal of the JNA units from BH, and the return of JNA members, soldiers and officers born in BH to their land of birth, Mirko Trivic was still serving in the land force military academy of JNA in May. Mirko Trivic started at the VRS personnel organ in Han Pijesak on 8th of January, 1993. The group of officers with him at the rear command post received an order and task from the president of the Serbian Republic of BH to form the Guards Motorised Brigade. Units were manned extra territorially by soldiers from the entire VRS -- entire Republika Srpska, from all VRS corps. The first official parade of the 1st Guards Motorised Brigade was on January the 19th, 1993. It was responsible for offensive task of the VRS in all operations in 1993, which were carried out successfully, contributing to the improvement of the strategic position of the Republika Srpska. On 8th of January, 1993, a large group of active servicemen arrived from Belgrade to Zvornik to man a VRS units. Mirko Trivic and his group were transferred under heavily armed escort. VRS units were unsuccessful achieving an important strategic goal in -- in 1992, which was to establish a corridor in Podrinje and connect with Herzegovina. I suppose it was successful. In January 1993, the process of formation and development of the organisation and establishment of the commanding of the VRS was not yet completed. Military units in Podrinje that were most fragmented were placed under a single command and the operation -- at the operations level. The Manoeuvre Brigade 1st Guard Brigade was subsequently formed, except for -- except some units in the 1st Krajina Corps. No VRS units were capable of carrying out offensive operations in an area outside their own municipality. All other brigades were formed out of municipality Territorial Defence into Light Infantry Brigades with territorial character and were intended for the protection of their municipality from well-organised Muslim military forces. In 1991, most VRS units were classified according to their combat experience as Territorial Defence sent units whose engagement evolved into the practice of weekend war, so-called weekend war in shifts. All other units remained fully manned after the withdrawal of JNA units from BH. This was particularly pronounced in the manning of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps which counted 2500 men after the withdrawal of Yugoslav citizens. Mobilisation into JNA units was carried out based on an extra territorial principle. Units mobilised as JNA units in BH up to that point were suddenly under manned. The Serb Territorial Defence was the backbone of the VRS units. The commitment of the political and military leadership of Serbs in BH to the struggle for fair military and political goals and the unity of Republika Srpska in BH is confirmed by the ethnic diversity among officers, active officers, serving in the VRS in 1992 and their motivation to participate in that struggle. Insufficient organisation, combat ability, and experience in armed combat in 1992 resulted in a large number of casualties among members of the Serbian army, and amongst civilians at all ages and sexes in villages with Serbs situated next to the area captured by the Muslim or Bosnian Croat forces. Victims were killed in situations where they could not run away while working the land, et cetera. These incidents escalated in 1992 and 1993 in Bratunac and Srebrenica. To stabilise the situation and prevents a pogrom and the drawing of the Serbian population out, the VRS carried out its first offensive operation in Konjevic Polje and Srebrenica. Future task of VRS in 1993, which ensured that from the strategic goals on current political goals in the war included preventing BH Army forces from committing crimes in the Zepa and Gorazde sector, liberating the corridor on the Dobro Polje route and road connecting Republika Srpska stabilising defence lines and preventing incidents in -- and ambushes in Serbian settlements. Regarding participation in military operations, in Podrinje 1993, the VRS forces were never given the objective to force out the Muslim population from Srebrenica. In addition to the significant military success of the VRS, the superior command did not assign a task to the units to force the Muslim population from Srebrenica. Regarding preparation and participation in operation Krivaja, the brigade did not hold contact lines with the Muslim forces. And the Serbian religious holiday in Vidovdan, Radovan Karadzic asked Mirko Trivic what to do -- what do you think about establishing a special operative command and VRS task force for the enclaves in Podrinje? Because this state of affairs is not good and nobody is responsible for the state of affairs in this area. Radovan Karadzic wanted to prevent more terrorist attacks by the BH Army, even if the goal of operation Krivaja was achieved and to consolidate the VRS defence around the enclaves. The Supreme Command did not think that the Srebrenica enclave should disappear. As such, no plan was ever adopted to eliminate the Bosnian Muslims from Srebrenica. And that would be the short summary. At that moment, I do not have questions for Colonel Trivic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the summary, Mr. Karadzic, you stated that Radovan Karadzic wanted to prevent more terrorist attack by the BiH army even if the goal of operation Krivaja was achieved and to consolidate the VRS defence around the enclaves. Is it coming from what paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite honest, at this moment, I don't know. I need to take a look, because I didn't actually refer to paragraph numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Perhaps I can assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's not directly from this paragraph but it's paragraph 2.6.2 at page 15 of the English is a supposition by the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's coming directly from that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's right [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- and it's related to your mens rea, so to speak. I would like you to deal with the witness live only that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, I would like to ask you what you knew about the political objectives and positions of the Supreme Commander and the Supreme Command in relation to the outcome, military outcome, of this conflict. What was it that we had wished for, what was it that we had advised?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I did not fully understand your question. Does it pertain to my summary or my statement, or generally speaking to political objectives? But if you allow me, I listened to the interpretation into the Serbian language of the summary that you read out and there were some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Forget about it. Forget about the summary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not the text. It's just my duties. It's not the text. It's not my statement. Did I not work at the personnel organ. I reported to the personnel organ in Han Pijesak. And secondly, in operation Krivaja, I was not serving in the guards brigade. I was serving in the 2nd Romanija Brigade. In that summary of yours, Mr. President, that was not pointed out. And now, back to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it was that you knew about the positions that I had in relation to the war and the resolution of the crisis?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Even before joining the Army of Republika Srpska, which came at my personal request, but there was also an order transferring me to serve in the Army of Republika Srpska, the positions of the Supreme Command and the political and military leadership were something that I was fully aware of. That is to say defence of the parts of the territory where the Serb people live in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in keeping with that, equal participation in decision making as a constituent people in Bosnia-Herzegovina about the position and the functioning of that state, or at the outset in 1992 before the declaration of independence, that is to say before the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that Bosnia-Herzegovina should remain functionally linked to some Yugoslavia, so some Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where representatives of all peoples would live in an equitable state. Since this did not happen in 1992, the objective of the Serb people was to participate in the functioning of that state as a constituent people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what your understanding was of my position in relation to the enclaves, the eastern enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, in view of what happened to them and around them?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.
